The hall was silent, with only the flickering candlelight reflecting off the memorial tablet enshrined in the center. It belonged to his late wife, Cui Mingyu’s mother.

He placed the oil lamp before the tablet, knelt down slowly, and pressed his palms together, two lines of aged tears rolling down once more: "My lady, do you see? Our Mingzhu is sensible now."

"It must be your spirit in heaven that sent her that dream, which is why she could wake up so quickly." His voice was choked with endless gratitude and relief. "Rest assured, I will take good care of her and protect her from now on. I will make sure she marries into a good family and lives a peaceful life. You can be at ease on the other side."

The candlelight danced, illuminating the white hair at his temples and the four elegant characters on the tablet, "Late Wife, Lady Su," as if silently responding to his words.

chapters.title: Princess Chao Gui
chapters.content:
The next day, the sun had already climbed high, casting gilded light through the carved window lattices of the Shangshu Mansion’s east courtyard onto the canopy bed draped in cloud brocade. Cui Mingyu turned over, her nose twitching, and slowly opened her eyes. She had never been one to struggle with sleeping in new places, even after transmigrating to this strange era.

She propped herself up on the brocade quilt to sit, and her personal maid, Qinghe, was already waiting in the outer room, entering softly upon hearing movement. After washing up, the little maid brought in breakfast—crystal dumplings, crab roe congee, and several dishes of refreshing pickles, all of which the original owner had loved. Cui Mingyu ate and drank slowly, digesting the memories in her mind that were not her own, occasionally asking Qinghe about the situation in the mansion in a calm manner. The original owner had been spoiled and headstrong, with her heart entirely set on the Prince of Jingnan, Wei Songjun, and she had been quite ignorant of the mundane affairs of the household. Now that she occupied this body, she had to thoroughly understand her surroundings.

Just as she was speaking with Qinghe, a series of hurried footsteps came from outside the courtyard, and Chuntao ran in, panting: "Miss! People from the Princess’s mansion are here! They say... they say the Princess requests your presence, and that you must go immediately!"

"The Princess?" Cui Mingyu’s heart stirred, and she reacted instantly. The person in the capital who would be in such a rush to summon her must be the young widow, Princess Chao Gui.

The memories regarding this Princess were vague in the original owner’s mind, leaving only a delicate outline: fair skin, pale lips, appearing weak and boneless, yet with a hint of coquettish charm hidden in her brows, and a gaze that could make anyone unable to look away. But what concerned Cui Mingyu most was that the packet of medicine the original owner had used on Wei Songjun had been gifted by this very Princess, and even the timing of the drugging had been hinted at by her.

The original owner had been obsessed with pursuing Wei Songjun and had followed Princess Chao Gui’s words blindly, never questioning why the Princess would help her. Cui Mingyu rubbed her fingertips, a sense of suspicion rising in her heart: Princess Chao Gui had been a widow for many years and kept many handsome male favorites in her mansion. Although there was gossip in the capital, no one dared to truly speak out. Such behavior inexplicably reminded her of the term "Black Widow," adding a chill to her heart.

Now that the Princess was summoning her in such a hurry, the intention was obvious—she surely wanted to know if the affair with Wei Songjun had succeeded yesterday. Cui Mingyu could not fathom the Princess’s mind; was she merely looking for entertainment, or did she have an ulterior motive?

She could not refuse a summons from the Princess. Half an hour later, Cui Mingyu sat in the Shangshu Mansion’s carriage as it rolled slowly toward the Princess’s mansion. The wheels ground against the bluestone road with a rhythmic clatter. She lifted a corner of the curtain, watched the flow of people on the street, and took a deep breath. Since she was here, she would make the best of it; no matter what Princess Chao Gui was planning, she could only take it one step at a time.

When the carriage arrived at the Princess’s mansion, Cui Mingyu passed through layers of vermilion corridors and lush greenery, heading deep into the grounds. The leading maid walked with a light step, guiding her around a rockery, when the view suddenly opened up—an exquisite white jade pavilion stood in the center of a pond. On the winding corridor connecting to the pavilion, two rows of handsome men stood in unison. They were all tall and slender, dressed in uniform moon-white robes, with gentle and mild expressions, devoid of any aggression, though their gazes carried a hint of curiosity as they fell upon Cui Mingyu.

Cui Mingyu’s cheeks grew slightly warm, and she subconsciously lowered her eyes. Although she came from the modern era and was used to all kinds of people, being stared at by two rows of handsome men still made her feel uneasy.

The maid led her onto the corridor, the white jade tiles beneath her feet as smooth as a mirror, reflecting her slightly flustered figure. As she reached the entrance of the pavilion, she saw snow-white gauze curtains hanging within, fluttering gently in the breeze. Behind the curtains, a slender figure could be vaguely seen reclining on a daybed in a lazy posture.

"Since you’ve come, why not come over?"

A voice suddenly drifted from behind the curtains, crisp as an oriole leaving the valley, yet wrapped in a cat-like laziness. The tail of the tone lifted slightly, carrying an indescribable allure.

Cui Mingyu paused, realizing the words were meant for her. She quickly composed herself, bowed, and saluted: "Your subject, Cui Mingyu, greets the Princess."

"Why so formal today? Come in."

Cui Mingyu stepped into the pavilion as instructed, the gauze curtains brushing against her sleeves with a faint, cool fragrance. Not daring to look around, she lowered her head and walked to the tea table, sitting gently in the empty seat opposite Princess Chao Gui. Her earlobes, however, remained flushed from the gazes on the corridor.

Only then did she dare to look at the person on the daybed. Princess Chao Gui was wearing a simple white cross-collared dress with faint orchid patterns embroidered on the hem. Her hair was styled in a simple 'following-the-clouds' bun, held only by a single mutton-fat jade hairpin. Her face, devoid of makeup, had skin as white and lustrous as jade, appearing even more translucent than the snow-white gauze curtains beside the bed. Such beauty was almost ostentatious, yet her plain clothes and lazy posture added a fragile, delicate quality. The two temperaments intertwined, making one afraid to look directly, yet unable to look away.

Seeing her sit, Princess Chao Gui frowned slightly, then a mischievous smile spread across her lips. Her gaze fell on Cui Mingyu’s flushed cheeks, filled with playful mockery: "You’re actually blushing? What, did things... succeed with the Prince of Jingnan last night?"

The question was direct and bold. Cui Mingyu’s heart jumped, and she subconsciously tightened her grip on her skirt. Just as she was hesitating on how to respond, Princess Chao Gui rose from the daybed, her bare feet stepping on the cool white jade tiles, and sat down at the tea table. She raised a hand to pour a cup of tea for her and gestured for her to drink: "Don't be in such a hurry to be shy. Tell me, what exactly happened last night? I’ve been waiting all morning for news."

At this moment, her eyes were bright, and her tone was full of curiosity, just like a young girl chasing after gossip—a stark contrast to the "Black Widow" image Cui Mingyu had imagined earlier.

Cui Mingyu picked up the teacup and steadied her nerves. Weighing her words to avoid the truth of her transmigration, she spoke slowly: "Princess, last night... nothing happened between the Prince of Jingnan and me. Furthermore, from now on, I will no longer be obsessed with the Prince."

"Why?" The smile on Princess Chao Gui’s face froze instantly. She was clearly stunned, then frowned, her tone filled with confusion: "Just because it didn't happen in one night, you’re giving up? What went wrong? The medicine I gave you... it was absolutely fine." Halfway through, she paused and changed her tone: "Since the medicine was fine, then the person must be the problem!"

As soon as she finished speaking, she leaned in close to Cui Mingyu, her phoenix eyes burning with intensity, staring straight into her eyes. The gaze was too sharp, as if it could pierce through a person’s heart. Cui Mingyu’s heart tightened suddenly, and it began to pound wildly—could it be that with just one sentence, Princess Chao Gui had realized she wasn't the original owner?

She was so nervous that her palms were sweating. Just as she was thinking about how to cover it up, she heard Princess Chao Gui’s red lips part, her tone filled with curiosity and certainty: "Could it be... that fellow Wei Songjun is actually... impotent?"

Cui Mingyu looked up abruptly, meeting the genuine confusion in Princess Chaogui’s eyes. For a moment, she didn’t know how to respond. Whether Wei Songjun was... or wasn’t... she certainly had no say in the matter, but it wouldn’t be right to pin such a label on a man without cause. Blushing, she clarified, “I don’t think... he is.”

“Don’t think?” With dry wood meeting fire and even aphrodisiacs involved, nothing had come of it, and it had even caused Cui Mingyu, who had always been obsessed with Wei Songjun, to lose interest. Chaogui couldn’t think of a second reason. Seeing Cui Mingyu’s reaction, she became even more certain of her guess. She curled her lip, her tone tinged with disdain: “I thought he was some golden, precious figure, but he turns out to be nothing more than a pretty face that’s useless! It’s a pity for you, having been nervous for nothing.” As she spoke, she leaned closer to Cui Mingyu and lowered her voice: “How about I introduce you to a few others? The ones in my manor are no worse than Wei Songjun—they have decent looks and gentle temperaments...”

Cui Mingyu was dumbfounded and quickly waved her hands: “Princess, you’re joking. This subject... this subject has no such intentions.”

Princess Chaogui raised an eyebrow. Watching her flustered appearance, she suddenly burst into laughter. The smile was bright and charming, completely devoid of the sharpness from moments before: “I truly don’t have anyone here whose looks can compare to Wei Songjun’s, but that doesn’t mean there aren’t any elsewhere. I, this Princess, will help you scout some out. But honestly, are you really planning to give up on Wei Songjun? You used to be willing to risk your life for him.”

Cui Mingyu lowered her eyes, masking the emotions in her gaze, and said softly: “In the past, I was too stubborn. After what happened yesterday, I finally understood that a twisted melon is not sweet. Since His Highness has no interest in me, there is no need for me to continue making a fool of myself.”

Chaogui looked thoughtful. She picked up her teacup, took a sip, and tilted her head: “That’s fine, it’s good to give up. That fellow Wei Songjun is indeed not a good match. A useless, embroidered pillow that looks good but lacks substance—he’s truly not worth you putting in this much effort.”

Cui Mingyu said: “Princess, regarding what happened yesterday, I beg you to keep it a secret for me, as if it never happened.”

Chaogui smiled cunningly and tapped the tabletop lightly with her fingertip: “Rest assured, I, this Princess, know best what should and shouldn’t be said.”

Seeing Chaogui’s smile, Cui Mingyu inwardly cried out that it was over. This smile was too much like her gossiping roommates—the look of someone who feared the world wouldn’t be chaotic enough. If Chaogui spread it around, Wei Songjun would be the first to not let her off the hook!

chapters.title: Bestowing Medicine
chapters.content:
When Cui Mingyu stepped out of the vermilion gates of the Princess’s manor, the sunlight outside was bright, yet it could not dispel the gloom between her brows. She raised a hand to tuck a slightly disheveled pearl hairpin behind her ear. Thinking of Princess Chaogui’s knowing, mocking eyes, her heart felt heavy, and she couldn’t help but let out a long sigh.

Yesterday’s events were meant to be a secret between her and Wei Songjun. She had thought it would be known to no one, but who would have expected Princess Chaogui to appear out of nowhere. She sighed lightly, leaned on Chuntao’s hand, and boarded the carriage, hoping only that this golden-branched, jade-leaved princess would heed her repeated pleas and keep this secret for her, and not go provoking Wei Songjun again.

The carriage wheels ground over the bluestone road, driving all the way into the Shangshu Manor. Cui Mingyu sat quietly in her room for half a day, her mind filled with the cold, sharp look in Wei Songjun’s eyes—he had said, “This does not mean the merits and faults cancel each other out.” The pressure in that tone still made her back feel cold even now.

As dusk fell and the clapper sounded for dinner in the front hall, Cui Mingyu composed herself and went to dine with her father.

Suddenly, Cui Yong set down his chopsticks, his tone tinged with the casual air of small talk: “Speaking of which, the morning court today was quite strange; the Prince of Jingnan didn’t show up.”

Cui Mingyu’s hand, holding her chopsticks, paused imperceptibly, then she nonchalantly put the vegetable into her mouth.

Cui Yong’s gaze swept over Cui Mingyu, probing. “They said his chronic headache flared up, and he had already submitted a leave request to the Emperor. The Prince of Jingnan has always been diligent; unless he was severely ill, he never missed court. I fear this time, he has been overworking himself for too long.” In the past, the whole manor knew of his daughter’s feelings for Wei Songjun. Let alone Wei Songjun being ill, even if it were rumored he had caught a cold, she would have spent the night turning over the storehouse, packing up ginseng, snow lotus, and other rare medicinal herbs, eager to deliver them to the Prince of Jingnan’s manor herself. But today, Cui Mingyu only gave a faint “Oh,” not even moving an eyebrow, as if they were discussing a stranger of no consequence.

Cui Yong was secretly delighted. It seemed his daughter had truly given up on the Prince of Jingnan; this was a good thing. He didn’t ask further and turned to discuss other official business.

Cui Mingyu’s face was calm and unruffled, but her heart had sunk to the bottom. A headache? She knew better than anyone that Wei Songjun wasn’t suffering from a headache at all, but was suffering from the effects of the aphrodisiac the original owner had used. Was the drug’s potency that overbearing? That after tossing and turning all night, he still couldn’t manage to attend the morning court? Her fingertips tightened slightly, and countless thoughts raced through her mind: Would Wei Songjun count this entire debt against her? With his temperament, would he take the opportunity to retaliate against the Cui family? That sentence, “Don’t think about canceling out merits and faults,” echoed repeatedly in her ears, making her feel even more restless.

She suppressed the panic in her heart, finished her meal in silence, and excused herself to her room. Standing by the window, looking at the waning moon in the sky, Cui Mingyu prayed in a low voice: Heavens and Buddhas, please bless the Prince of Jingnan to get well soon, and please, do not let him vent his anger on me.

But she never expected that Wei Songjun’s illness would last for a full half-month.

During this half-month, Cui Mingyu lived every day with her heart in her throat. Whenever the servants in the manor discussed the Prince of Jingnan’s condition, she would pretend to listen unintentionally. From the initial “The Prince’s manor is closed tight, seeing no outsiders,” to later, “I heard the Prince can get out of bed and walk,” and then to, “Why is he still not attending court? Could it be that he’s left behind a lingering illness?” Every comment was like a stone, smashing into her heart.

“Is his body naturally weak, or is that drug really that potent?” Cui Mingyu sat before her vanity, murmuring to her own slightly haggard face in the bronze mirror. Half a month without attending court—this was unprecedented for the diligent Wei Songjun, showing that he must have been severely drained that day. The more she thought, the more afraid she became, feeling that Wei Songjun would certainly not let it go and might be biding his time to deal with her.

Another day, hearing that there was still no movement from the Prince of Jingnan’s manor, Cui Mingyu leaned against the window frame and let out a long sigh, her eyes full of helplessness. She hadn’t enjoyed many peaceful days since transmigrating, and she had already landed in such a mess. Truly, her fate was full of twists and turns, and her life was as insignificant as dust.

But then she thought, Wei Songjun hadn’t sent anyone to find her in these fifteen days. Perhaps... he really intended to let her go? The moment this thought emerged, Cui Mingyu suppressed it herself. Who was Wei Songjun? He was the Prince of Jingnan, a man of great military achievements and deep, calculating thoughts. How could he so easily forgive someone who had schemed against him?

After the half-month passed, Cui Mingyu finally received news: Wei Songjun had recovered and was attending court.

Cui Mingyu was practicing calligraphy at the time. Upon hearing this, her brush paused, leaving a crooked ink blot on the rice paper. She set down the brush, her palms slightly cold—was he... going to start settling the score? How would he deal with her?

At this moment in the Imperial Palace, after the morning court ended, the Emperor specifically kept Wei Songjun in the Imperial Study to discuss matters. Between the reorganization of water transport and border defense, one state affair after another was discussed, and it was nearly noon. Wei Songjun bowed to take his leave. Just as he walked out of the vermilion gates of the Imperial Study, he saw Princess Chaogui, accompanied by a group of palace maids and eunuchs, strolling over from the covered walkway.

The summer sun shone on Chaogui. She was wearing a pomegranate-red floral gauze dress, swaying gracefully as she walked. When she approached, her gaze unabashedly scanned Wei Songjun from head to toe, a meaningful smile curling the corners of her lips.

Wei Songjun’s heart tightened slightly, but his face maintained the respect of a subject. He stepped back two paces and bowed: “This subject greets the Princess.”

Chaogui did not stop, stepping forward two paces until she was almost face-to-face with him. The incense on her was overly sweet and cloying, making Wei Songjun frown subconsciously and move half an inch to the side, maintaining distance.

“The Prince of Jingnan need not be so formal.” Chaogui’s voice was coquettish, but her eyes were glued to him. “This Princess is just curious: has the Prince’s illness fully recovered?”

Wei Songjun nodded faintly, his tone distant: “Thanks to the Princess’s concern, it has recovered.” He did not want to entangle himself with this notoriously willful princess and only wanted to leave as soon as possible.

But Chaogui had no intention of letting him go. She blinked, the smile at the corners of her eyes deepening, the mockery in her tone almost overflowing: “Is that so?”

The strangeness in that tone made Wei Songjun’s heart sink. He couldn’t be bothered to speculate further and bowed again: “This subject has urgent matters at the manor, I shall take my leave.” With that, he turned to go.

Chaogui suddenly chuckled. As he brushed past her, she leaned in slightly and said in a voice only the two of them could hear: “So... has this impotence also been cured?”

With a “swish,” Wei Songjun’s footsteps stopped abruptly. He spun around, the calm on his face instantly shattering, replaced by sheer astonishment. Then, his eyes narrowed, a cold glint appearing, and the air pressure around him dropped instantly. His tone was as cold as ice: “Princess, watch your words!”

But Chaogui completely ignored the danger in his eyes. Instead, she stepped back, leaning against a pillar, lazily fiddling with the jade bracelet on her wrist: “Why must the Prince of Jingnan lose his temper? If you’re ill, you must seek treatment; you cannot hide your illness for fear of the doctor.”

Wei Songjun stared fixedly at Chaogui, his eyes dark and gloomy. He instantly guessed where this absurd rumor had come from. During the half-month he spent recovering, he had thought that since Cui Mingyu had admitted her mistake and stopped in time, not causing a major disaster, he would let her off for now. But he hadn’t expected her to be so reckless as to dare to use such a thing to frame him!

The hostility around him was almost overflowing. His fingers curled slightly, suppressing the rage in his heart. But then he thought, such matters only become darker the more you try to wipe them clean. If he argued with Chaogui in public, it would only let more people hear it, and by the time the gossip spread throughout the capital, it would be counterproductive. Although he, Wei Songjun, did not fear gossip, this concerned his dignity as a man, and there was no way to prove his innocence. It would be better to treat it with cold indifference.

A moment later, the cold glint in Wei Songjun’s eyes gradually faded, and a mocking smile curled his lips instead. He looked at Chaogui, his tone calm but tinged with playfulness: “Many thanks for the Princess’s concern. Come to think of it, that ‘divine medicine’ the Princess bestowed that day was quite useful. Could you bestow some more upon this subject?”

Chaogui was stunned, then a satisfied smile appeared on her face. In her view, Wei Songjun’s words were undoubtedly an admission of the “impotence” rumor, only he was too embarrassed to say it clearly. She lifted her chin triumphantly: “Rest assured, this Princess is best at keeping secrets and won’t spread it. I’ll have someone send that medicine to your manor later; it’s guaranteed to work.”

Wei Songjun did not respond, only looked at her deeply—a gaze complex and unreadable—then bowed again: “In that case, I thank the Princess. This subject takes his leave.”

chapters.title: Begging for Mercy
chapters.content:
As the evening clouds descended, the bustle of the capital gradually faded. In the courtyard of the Prince of Jingnan’s manor, the steward hurried in holding a translucent white porcelain bottle, bowed, and said: “Your Highness, the medicine sent by Princess Chaogui has arrived.”

Wei Songjun was standing by the window, watching the paulownia trees in the courtyard, when he turned around at the sound of footsteps. The porcelain bottle was small and delicate, its glaze smooth and lustrous. He reached out to take it, weighing it in his hand, a faint ripple of emotion crossing his eyes. It was the medicine in this very bottle that had forced him to recuperate for half a month. He rubbed the intricate patterns on the bottle and said in a low voice, "Summon Qin Yi."

Before long, the dark-clad guard Qin Yi arrived, his posture as straight as a pine. He lowered his head and awaited orders: "What are your instructions, Your Highness?"

"Go to the residence of Minister Cui," Wei Songjun said, placing the porcelain bottle on the table. "Invite Cui Mingyu to come here. If she refuses, bring her by force."

Qin Yi looked up abruptly, his stern expression nearly faltering. Having served Wei Songjun for many years, he knew all too well his master’s attitude toward the young lady of the Cui household. In the past, Cui Mingyu had pursued him so openly that the entire capital knew of it, yet Wei Songjun had avoided her like a plague, never even accepting the invitations sent by the Cui residence. This uncharacteristic order left him completely bewildered. However, he dared not ask further and simply bowed, replying, "As you command, sir."

At the Cui residence, dinner had just concluded. Cui Mingyu was lounging on a soft couch, having her shoulders massaged by her maid, Bitao, with unfinished osmanthus cake still on the table. Her father had gone to a banquet with his colleagues, and the house was uncharacteristically quiet. She had just let out a sigh of relief when the gatekeeper ran in, flustered: "Miss! Someone from the Prince Jingnan’s residence is here, saying the Prince requests your immediate presence!"

With a "clatter," the bowl of honey water in Cui Mingyu’s hand fell onto the couch, spilling over half her skirt without her even noticing. She sat bolt upright, the color draining from her small face, her heart sinking like a lead weight. The sword that had been hanging over her head for so long had finally fallen.

Suppressing her panic, she smoothed her skirt and walked to the front hall. Seeing Qin Yi standing there expressionless, the sword at his waist glinting with a cold, menacing light, she felt even more intimidated. "Sir," she said, forcing a gentle smile despite her trembling voice, "it is already dark. For a young woman to go to the Prince's residence alone might damage the Prince's reputation if word gets out. Could I not pay my respects in person first thing tomorrow morning?"

Qin Yi stood with his arms crossed, his tone unyielding: "Miss Cui, the Prince has given his orders. If you refuse to go, I have no choice but to bring you by force." He muttered to himself: In the past, this Miss Cui would chase the Prince’s carriage for half a street without tiring; why does she act like she’s seen a tiger today? The minds of these two are truly hard to fathom.

Cui Mingyu’s face fell, bitter as gall. She knew no one dared defy Wei Songjun’s orders, so she bit her lip and plotted. Catching Qin Yi off guard, she tugged on Chuntao’s sleeve and whispered, "Go find my father quickly and tell him to get me out of Prince Jingnan’s residence."

Chuntao understood, but just as she turned to run toward the backyard, Qin Yi drew his sword with a "shing," the blade pointing at the ground with a chilling gleam. "Eek!" Chuntao jumped back, her face deathly pale, stammering, "W-why are you drawing your weapon? That’s terrifying!"

Qin Yi sheathed his sword, his tone remaining cold and hard: "The Prince said, Miss Cui, don’t play any tricks. Everyone must answer for their own actions; don’t drag others into this."

Cui Mingyu sighed, knowing her last hope was gone. She turned to Qinghe and instructed, "I am going to the Prince's residence. You stay by the gate. If my father returns, tell him I was feeling unwell and went to sleep; do not let a word slip." Bitao immediately grabbed her hand, her eyes red: "Miss, I’ll go with you! I’ll stay by your side!"

But as she took a step forward, Qin Yi blocked her. Bitao’s eyes welled up with tears, looking like a wronged little puppy as she gazed pitifully at Cui Mingyu.

Seeing her clumsy but loyal maid, Cui Mingyu felt a warmth in her heart and patted her hand: "Be good, go back with Qinghe. I’ll be fine." After finally coaxing Bitao away, she pulled her cloak tight and braced herself to step into the Prince Jingnan’s carriage.

The carriage wheels rumbled over the bluestone road, but to Cui Mingyu, the sound was drowned out by the thumping of her own heart. She peered out the window at the passing streetlights, her mind a tangled mess: What did Wei Songjun want? Was he going to beat her? Punish her? Or... take her life? She even absurdly hoped the road would never end, but that thought was as futile as expecting Wei Songjun to let her go.

Before long, it seemed in the blink of an eye, the carriage stopped. Cui Mingyu lifted the curtain to see the towering vermilion gates of the Prince Jingnan’s residence, the stone lions on either side glaring with an imposing, keep-out aura. She took a deep breath to steady herself: *Cui Mingyu, don’t be afraid! He said he would spare your life; he can’t go back on his word!* Yet her legs felt like lead, shaking uncontrollably, and she moved slower than a snail.

Qin Yi followed behind, growing impatient and wishing he could just carry her into the house. After finally shuffling to the entrance of the main hall, Qin Yi announced her and then tactfully withdrew, closing the door behind him and shutting out the world.

The hall was lit only by a few palace lanterns, the warm yellow light casting a glow on Wei Songjun. He wore a navy blue silk robe embroidered with dark gold cloud patterns, sitting upright in the master’s chair. His brow was furrowed, his eyes downcast as he rubbed the porcelain bottle on the table. Hearing footsteps, he looked up, his gaze as sharp as an eagle’s, landing squarely on Cui Mingyu.

Cui Mingyu shivered under his gaze, her knees turning to jelly, and she nearly collapsed. She grabbed a nearby pillar to steady herself. The hall was deathly quiet, save for the sound of her own frantic heartbeat; she didn't even dare to breathe too loudly.

After a long stalemate, Cui Mingyu finally found her voice, her tone trembling as she whispered, "Y-Your Highness, you previously said... you would spare my life."

Wei Songjun raised an eyebrow, looking coldly at the young girl before him. In the past, she was always dressed gaudily, chasing after him like a high-spirited little sparrow, arrogant and flamboyant. But today, she was hunched over, head bowed, the pearl hairpin on her temple askew, looking like a drenched little quail. He raised an eyebrow, his voice icy: "Do you know what it means to say 'a death sentence may be avoided, but a living punishment is hard to escape'?"

"A-a living punishment?" Cui Mingyu shivered in terror, visions of whips and canes flashing through her mind. Her knees gave way, and she fell to the cold brick floor with a thud. It hurt, but she didn't dare rub it, instead looking up with a pale, pitiful face to plead: "Your Highness, I am frail; I cannot withstand such torment! If you accidentally break me, wouldn't you be breaking your word? You are the noble Prince Jingnan; you must keep your promise!"

Wei Songjun frowned even deeper at her spineless display, his tone darkening: "Get up!"

Cui Mingyu hesitated, her eyes red as she begged: "Your Highness, you are a man of great stature, please spare me this once. I truly know I was wrong!"

Wei Songjun did not answer, only pointing to the porcelain bottle on the table and saying coldly, "Come here."

Cui Mingyu felt uneasy but dared not disobey. She pushed herself up and walked to the table with unsteady steps. She curiously glanced at the bottle, finding it somewhat familiar, as if she had seen it somewhere before.

"What is this?" she couldn't help but ask in a low voice.

"You don't recognize it?" Wei Songjun picked up the bottle.

Memories of the original owner surfaced. Cui Mingyu remembered: this was... this was the aphrodisiac Princess Chao Gui had given the original owner. How did it end up in Wei Songjun’s hands?

chapters.title: Revenge
chapters.content:
Wei Songjun twirled the medicine bottle between his fingertips, his ink-black eyes swirling with undisguised playfulness and malice. His gaze, like an ice-tempered hook, locked firmly onto Cui Mingyu. "Recognize it now?" His tone was flat but carried an undeniable pressure. He tilted his wrist, handing the bottle directly to her. "Drink it."

Cui Mingyu stiffened, subconsciously stumbling half a step back. She wasn't foolish enough to think this powerful Prince Jingnan had ulterior motives for her; the hatred in his eyes was too raw. He simply wanted her to experience the same torment he had suffered that day.

Her hands, hanging at her sides, clenched tightly, her nails digging into her palms to steady herself with the sharp pain. She wiped the dried tears from her cheeks, sniffled, and with a voice raspy from crying, tried to bargain with him: "Your Highness, if I drink this, can the debt between us be wiped clean?"

"Wiped clean?" Wei Songjun let out a cold, mocking laugh, as if he had heard the greatest joke in the world. Princess Chao Gui’s remark about him being "impotent" still echoed in his ears, every word piercing his heart like a needle—and the root of it all was this woman before him. The air pressure around him plummeted, a murderous aura rising like a physical force. "Cui Mingyu, you have no right to bargain with me. That you are still standing here breathing is only due to the meager bit of worthless mercy I have left. Do not challenge my bottom line."

The murderous intent stifled her breath. She had no doubt that if she said "no," she would be headless the next second. It was just an aphrodisiac; she could find someone to help her resolve it later, which was better than losing her life on the spot. She closed her eyes, and when she opened them, she was resolute. She took the cold bottle, pulled out the stopper, and tilted her head back, drinking the pale pink liquid in one gulp.

The liquid was slightly sweet at first, but it carried a burning aftertaste that slid down her throat, instantly igniting a small flame in her chest. She turned the empty bottle upside down and shook it to show it was finished. "Your Highness, may I go now?"

Wei Songjun did not move, his dark gaze fixed on her flushed cheeks, his tone as cold as ice: "Where do you think you're going?"

The medicine took effect faster than Cui Mingyu had anticipated. In just a moment, that small flame swept through her entire body like a wildfire. A rolling wave of heat surged from her limbs, her body burning, her throat so dry it felt like it might spit fire, and even the scene before her began to blur. She finally understood why, despite Wei Songjun’s formidable martial arts, he had been trapped by this very thing that day.

She bit her lower lip, struggling to maintain a shred of consciousness, and leaned against a pillar to steady herself. "Naturally, to find someone to help me resolve the poison." The first person to cross her mind was Xia Yuning—he had loved the original owner for years, and she didn't dislike him either. Besides, her father, Cui Yong, had always favored the Xia family. If something were to happen, marrying him afterward wouldn't be such a loss.

She stumbled toward the door, but her wrist was suddenly gripped by a powerful hand. Wei Songjun’s palm, calloused from years of sword practice, was much cooler than her burning skin. When he covered her hand, it felt like a cool breeze in midsummer, so comfortable she couldn't help but sigh. In her muddled state, Cui Mingyu grabbed his hand tightly and murmured, "So comfortable..."

"Presumptuous!" Wei Songjun’s expression changed drastically. He shoved her away as if burned, his tone filled with gnashing, visceral rage. "Cui Mingyu, do you think I gave you this medicine so you could go find another man to dally with?"

His force was immense. Cui Mingyu, already limp, was pushed backward, her lower back slamming heavily against the cold floor tiles. The bone-chilling cold seeped through her clothes, clearing her muddled mind slightly. She propped herself up with her arms and looked up at the man with the grim, dark expression before her, her voice trembling with restrained emotion. "Your Highness, I recall giving you two choices that day. It was you who insisted on maintaining your purity and refused to yield to anyone, choosing instead to soak in ice water to dispel the drug's effects. I do not claim to have your resolve; when given a choice, I naturally chose the first."

Wei Songjun laughed, but the mirth did not reach his eyes, leaving only cold mockery. He remembered the shocking words she had used that day, like "Fifth Miss," and knew then that she was a woman who knew no shame. To her, chastity was likely the least valuable thing; to avoid the torment of the drug, she would naturally choose to rely on another without hesitation.

Yet, he had gone to such lengths to bring her here, not to let her go off seeking pleasure.

"In your dreams." Wei Songjun stepped forward, looking down at her as she sprawled on the floor, his tone devoid of warmth. "You will soak in the ice water all night. If you can survive until dawn, then it is your good fortune. If you die, I have never been one to haggle with the dead, and it shall be considered as fulfilling your wish—a clean slate from here on out."

This was the outer parlor of the Prince's residence, a considerable distance from the bathing room on the west side. Cui Mingyu was already limp as mud, lacking even the strength to lift her arms. Cold sweat had soaked through her moon-white *ruqun*, clinging to her body and outlining her alluring curves.

Wei Songjun watched her, his heart sinking inexplicably. Having suffered the torment of this drug himself, he knew clearly how much she was suffering—it was his own lack of foresight; he should have thrown her directly into an ice barrel earlier, sparing him the trouble of dealing with her now.

He could have summoned the palace matrons to throw her into the tub, but for some reason, he did not want others to see her looking so soft and seductive.

After a moment of hesitation, Wei Songjun bent down and scooped Cui Mingyu up horizontally. Her body was lighter than he had imagined, her soft form pressed against him with a scorching heat. His nose was filled with the faint, fresh scent of gardenias on her skin, which had become even more intense after being soaked in sweat, winding around his senses like vines and making his heart itch inexplicably.

Cui Mingyu’s consciousness was already blurred. Feeling the solid, slightly cool embrace, she instinctively burrowed into his warm chest, rubbing her small face against his lapel and mumbling a name vaguely: "Xia Yuning..."

Xia Yuning?

Wei Songjun’s movements halted abruptly, his eyes instantly covered in thick frost. That chubby boy from the Xia family? Even in such a state, she was still thinking of another man? The inexplicable softness in his heart vanished instantly, replaced only by surging anger and malice. His footsteps heavy, he strode to the bathing room and, without waiting for Cui Mingyu to react, threw her fiercely into the tub already prepared and filled with shards of ice.

With a splash, the freezing water instantly engulfed Cui Mingyu. The bone-chilling cold collided with the scorching heat within her, bringing a tearing, excruciating pain. She couldn't help but let out a sharp, muffled groan, her vision darkening as she nearly fainted on the spot.

Wei Songjun stood by the tub, watching her body curl up in agony in the ice water, her face turning from flushed to deathly pale, her lips drained of color. Yet, he felt no satisfaction; instead, he felt as if something were blocking his chest, suffocating him. He said coldly, "Endure it well. This is what you owe me."

Cui Mingyu gritted her teeth, refusing to cry out. She only looked up at the cold man before her, letting the ice water soak her burning body. Every inch of her skin throbbed with the interplay of cold and heat. She was in too much pain to think, asking him only by instinct, "Wei Songjun, what exactly will it take for you to let me go?"

Wei Songjun looked down at her, his eyes devoid of warmth. His thin lips parted, his tone cold enough to crack the air: "When you understand what should be said and what should not, I will naturally let you go!"

What should be said? What should not?

Cui Mingyu’s mind was a chaotic mess, as if shrouded in thick fog, lost and helpless. What on earth had she said? For the past half-month, she had lived in seclusion, rarely stepping out of her doors. She had only seen Xia Yuning once and visited the Princess's residence once—what could she have possibly said to provoke such monstrous rage?

Wait... the Princess's residence!

A thought struck her chaotic mind like a thunderbolt. Cui Mingyu shuddered violently, her heart turning cold. It was over. Princess Chaogui must have gone to confront him about his "impotence."

chapters.title: Admitting Fault
chapters.content:
Daylight finally broke through the shackles of night, casting a faint, slanted glow through the lattice windows into the sparsely furnished side room. The heat that had been roasting Cui Mingyu’s bones—the lingering remnants of the aphrodisiac that had plagued her all night—finally faded, leaving behind an unexpected sense of emptiness.

But as the heat subsided, the cold that had settled in the tub clung to her like a parasite, surging from all directions, piercing through her soaked undergarments and wrapping tightly around her limbs and bones. Cui Mingyu couldn't help but shiver, her teeth chattering. She raised a hand to her forehead; the scorching heat against her palm made her heart sink, and she forced a bitter smile.

Soaking in an ice barrel all night, buffeted by heat and cold—it would be a miracle if she didn't have a fever.

She propped herself against the edge of the tub, trying to stand, but her head felt as heavy as lead. As soon as she straightened halfway, her legs gave way, and she nearly fell back into the water. In a panic, she gripped the edge of the tub, taking a long moment to steady herself. Her wet hair clung to her neck and cheeks, dripping with ice water, adding to the chill.

Looking down at her disheveled, soaked state, Cui Mingyu frowned. This was Wei Songjun’s Prince Jingnan’s residence. How was she to walk out of this room and return to her quarters in this state? Just as she was fretting, her peripheral vision caught sight of a set of neatly folded clothes on the screen beside the tub—plain silk fabric embroidered with a faint orchid pattern, clearly a woman's style.

At this point, she couldn't afford to question why the clothes were there. Cui Mingyu gritted her teeth and laboriously stripped off her wet garments, her fingers trembling from cold and weakness. She finally managed to change into the clean set. The clothes carried a faint scent of soap and fit surprisingly well, though she was so weak that she still swayed, having to lean against the screen to move.

Just as she cleared the screen, the sight before her made her heart jump, and she froze.

Sitting at the pear-wood table in front of the screen was a man. His black silk robe accentuated his tall, pine-like stature, his dark hair tied up with a jade crown, his side profile sharp and smooth. It was none other than Prince Jingnan, Wei Songjun. He had been sitting there for who knows how long; the tea in the cup had long since gone cold, and a low, oppressive pressure surrounded him, warning others to keep their distance.

Cui Mingyu’s cheeks flushed a faint red, shame and embarrassment washing over her. He must have heard every sound she made while changing. To be caught in such a private state—even though she had transmigrated into this book and was no longer the infatuated Cui family miss of the original story—still felt unbearable.

Wei Songjun slowly lifted his eyes, his gaze landing on her. His eyes were as deep as a cold pool, devoid of ripples, yet they precisely captured her bloodless face, her nearly transparent lips, and her weakness as she leaned against the screen to stand. He understood; she had suffered greatly from the drug last night.

Cui Mingyu’s head was still throbbing, her temples pulsing. She gripped the edge of the screen to support her swaying body and whispered, "Your Highness..."

As soon as she spoke, she was startled herself. Her voice was hoarse and dry, no longer the clear, bright tone she usually had; it sounded as if it had been rubbed with sandpaper, utterly unpleasant. She instinctively wanted to clear her throat, but the slightest effort brought a needle-like pain from deep within, as if an invisible string were pulling tight, causing heart-wrenching agony with every movement.

Misfortunes never come singly. Cui Mingyu inwardly forced a bitter smile. Enduring the pain in her throat, she looked at the expressionless Wei Songjun, her voice still hoarse: "Your Highness, may I leave now?"

Wei Songjun’s gaze grew colder, his tone devoid of warmth: "Do you know your mistake?"

Cui Mingyu wanted to nod, but her head felt as heavy as a thousand pounds; no matter how hard she tried, her neck wouldn't budge. Helpless, she could only blink, her eyes filled with a weak submissiveness: "I was wrong."

"Where were you wrong?" Wei Songjun pressed, the pressure in his voice intensifying.

Cui Mingyu steadied herself, struggling to organize her thoughts, and listed them one by one in her raspy voice: "I was wrong to foolishly covet Your Highness's favor, wrong to be muddled enough to drug you and cause you such agony... and even more wrong to mislead Princess Chaogui, leading her to suspect Your Highness's... physical condition."

When she reached the end, she dared not utter the words "impotence." The Princess's suspicion had already touched his raw nerve; to be so blunt now would only be adding fuel to the fire.

"Enough—"

Wei Songjun suddenly raised his hand, sweeping the cold tea off the table. The crisp sound of the porcelain cup shattering was jarring in the silent room. His eyes surged with rage, the cold air around him enough to freeze a person: "And have you thought of how to make amends? My life has been bright and upright; the only stain is you, Cui Mingyu! Killing you would not be enough to vent my anger!"

Cui Mingyu trembled at his rage, causing the screen she held to sway slightly. Her eyes turned red instantly, and her nose stung painfully.

The heavens were unfair! Why did it have to be her who transmigrated into this book? The original owner had pestered Wei Songjun for years, committing countless stupid acts. It was she who, after taking over, had carefully made amends to prevent things from becoming an irreparable disaster. Had she not suffered enough last night, being tortured by the drug and soaking in ice water? Now he wanted her to make amends—how could she? Was she supposed to find a Moonlight Box, turn back time, and erase all the original owner's mistakes?

She rubbed her heavy temples hard, suppressing the grievance in her heart, and said hoarsely, "Your Highness, I will personally explain to Princess Chaogui and clarify all misunderstandings. I will never let her suspect Your Highness again."

"How will you explain?" Wei Songjun raised an eyebrow, his tone laced with sarcasm and impatience.

His words were like a basin of ice water, sobering Cui Mingyu instantly, but a deeper sense of bewilderment followed. Yes, such matters were hard to speak of; how was she to explain? She feared she would only make things worse.

Her head grew heavier and heavier, the scene before her eyes began to blur, and Wei Songjun’s voice in her ears gradually faded into the distance. Cui Mingyu parted her lips, just about to say something more, when she felt the world spinning. Everything went black, and her body collapsed uncontrollably toward the floor.

The expected pain did not come; instead, she was caught in a warm, broad embrace. Before she completely lost consciousness, Cui Mingyu vaguely caught a faint scent of ambergris—the unique fragrance that belonged to Wei Songjun.

Wei Songjun looked down at the young girl in his arms, who felt as light as a feather, his brows furrowed tightly. Her originally pale face was now flushed with an unnatural crimson, forming a jarring contrast with her bloodless lips. Subconsciously, he raised his hand, and when his fingertips touched the temperature of her forehead, his gaze darkened abruptly.

*She’s burning up this badly.*

He mused to himself that the aphrodisiac was potent and caused immense damage to the body. Even with his robust constitution, it had taken him half a month to fully recover. Yesterday, he had deliberately reduced the dosage by more than half, but she was, after all, a weak woman with no strength to truss a chicken; how could she withstand the impact of the drug's potency? He had purged the drug from his system in just an hour, yet she had endured it for an entire night.

Wei Songjun held her, his footsteps pausing slightly as he was about to call for the manor physician, when the girl in his arms suddenly stirred.

She struggled to lift her heavy eyelids, her gaze unfocused and filled with deep confusion, like a child who had lost its way home. Her voice was hoarse, and her tone was full of reliance and grievance: "I want to go home... I don't want to be here..."

The voice was as light as a breeze, yet it inexplicably struck Wei Songjun’s heart.

chapters.title: Never Mention It Again
chapters.content:
Wei Songjun’s voice was as heavy as black iron: "You can’t even stand steady now, how can you go back? Let the manor physician examine you before you leave!"

Cui Mingyu struggled to push him away. Her force was extremely light; rather than resistance, it was more like she was holding onto her final shred of dignity. Her voice was thin and weak, yet clear: "Many thanks for the Prince’s kindness, but this subject’s daughter cannot afford to accept it. I am fine; I will be well after resting for a while."

Wei Songjun’s gaze darkened. His cold, piercing eyes swept over her paper-white face, the damp hair clinging to her forehead, and her spine, which was held stiffly upright despite her inability to stand steadily. This woman actually dared to give him the cold shoulder? By what right? Indignation surged within his chest. He pressed his thin lips into a line, let out a cold snort, and called out: "Qin Yi!"

Qin Yi, who was waiting not far away, immediately stepped forward quickly and bowed his head in readiness: "This subordinate is here."

"Send Miss Cui back to her manor." Wei Songjun’s voice lacked even a shred of warmth, every word sharp: "Remember, do not let her die in the Prince’s manor; it would soil my grounds. And do not let her die on the road, lest the Cui family turn around and accuse my Prince Jingnan’s manor of taking lives recklessly."

Cui Mingyu’s heart felt as if it had been pricked by these cold words. A dull pain spread, and her already muddled head grew even heavier; the figures and pillars before her twisted into a blurred mass. She gritted her teeth and bit down hard on the tip of her tongue. The sharp pain pierced through the chaos, barely granting her a moment of clarity. She bowed her head slightly, her voice as light as the wind, yet perfectly polite: "I trouble you, Master Qin."

Qin Yi stood where he was, his gaze darting quickly between his master and Miss Cui, a flicker of surprise rising in his heart. This side room was remote and rarely visited; he had not expected his master to be here with Miss Cui, and for things to have turned so sour. Miss Cui had been invited to the manor by him yesterday evening and had stayed for an entire night; the plain-colored *ruqun* she wore was also a different style—certainly not the one from yesterday. Seeing her so weak that she seemed as if a gust of wind could blow her over, Qin Yi could not help but harbor some guesses. Yet, looking at the tense, hostile atmosphere, there was not a shred of mutual affection to be seen.

However, in all the years he had followed Wei Songjun, Cui Mingyu was the first young woman to have stayed overnight in the manor. Such special treatment was certainly not that of an ordinary guest. Qin Yi immediately set aside the arrogance he had shown when going to the Cui manor to invite her yesterday, his attitude becoming more respectful as he cupped his hands: "Miss Cui is too polite. You may simply call me Qin Yi. Please, this way."

Cui Mingyu said nothing more and began to walk toward the manor gate. Every step felt like treading on cotton—feeble and powerless. She had to lean against a wall or a pillar to rest every few steps. Cold sweat trickled down from her temples, soaking the stray hairs, yet from beginning to end, she did not show weakness, nor did she look back at that cold gaze. Qin Yi followed patiently by her side without a word of urging, only moving discreetly closer when she nearly stumbled, though he dared not offer support, mindful of the boundaries between men and women.

After stumbling all the way to the carriage outside the manor gate, Cui Mingyu looked at the carriage shaft, which was not particularly high, but felt like a vast distance away. She gripped her sleeves tightly and tried to step up, but her legs were too weak to obey, and her body swayed. Seeing this, Qin Yi reached out in time and gently placed a hand on her elbow to provide support. Cui Mingyu did not refuse; using this force, she climbed onto the shaft and, as soon as she entered the carriage, could no longer hold on, collapsing heavily onto the soft cushions.

All her strength seemed to have been drained away. Cold sweat soaked her undergarments, sticking to her skin, feeling both cold and itchy. Her chest felt as if it were blocked by a giant boulder; every breath was labored and painful, and her throat felt scorched, making even swallowing saliva an unbearable torture. She leaned against the carriage wall, closing her eyes and panting for a long time before she recovered slightly. With a hoarse voice, she said to Qin Yi outside: "Master Qin, please take the back gate of the Cui manor."

She dared not use the main entrance. If her father, Cui Yong, were to run into her in this state and question her whereabouts after being away all night, it would surely lead to another storm. The original owner of this body had a lively personality and often slipped out through the back gate to play; at this hour, there should be maidservants guarding it.

Qin Yi replied with a "Very well" and ordered the coachman to change direction. The carriage traveled steadily for about two quarters of an hour before arriving at the back gate of the Cui manor. Sure enough, Qinghe and Bitao were pacing back and forth anxiously at the gate. Seeing the carriage stop, they immediately hurried forward. When they saw Qin Yi helping the frail and exhausted Cui Mingyu off the carriage, Bitao’s expression darkened instantly. She glared fiercely at Qin Yi as if her mistress had been bullied by him, then she and Qinghe supported Cui Mingyu by her arms, their voices urgent: "Miss! You’ve finally returned! What happened to you?"

Cui Mingyu shook her head weakly, having no strength to speak. She simply let the two maids support her into the manor and went straight to her own quarters.

As soon as she lay on the bed, she summoned her last bit of energy to instruct Qinghe: "Don't... don't tell my father I was away all night. Just say I caught a chill last night." After giving this instruction, everything went black, and she fell into a deep, unconscious sleep.

Seeing her mistress’s deathly pale face and touching her burning forehead, how could Qinghe dare to delay? She immediately turned and ran to the front hall to report to Cui Yong. Upon hearing that his daughter had caught a chill and was running a high fever, Cui Yong was frantic. He tossed his official documents aside and personally went to fetch the most famous physician in the city, Dr. Li, to the manor for treatment.

Brewing medicine, feeding water, wiping her body—the maids were kept busy off their feet. Cui Yong also kept watch outside the sickroom, asking about her condition every so often. After three full days of this ordeal, Cui Mingyu’s high fever finally subsided completely. However, her body had already been depleted, and having suffered such an ordeal, she remained extremely weak upon waking, lacking even the strength to lift her hand, and her complexion remained a sickly pale.

On the afternoon of that day, sunlight spilled through the window lattice onto the bed, bringing a gentle warmth. Suddenly, a maid’s voice came from outside the door: "Miss, Princess Chaogui has arrived to see you."

Cui Mingyu frowned slightly, then relaxed.

Princess Chaogui, dressed in a vibrant pomegranate-red palace gown, walked in quickly with several palace maids. Seeing the frail Cui Mingyu lying on the bed, she sighed immediately, hurried to the bedside, sat down, and reached out to gently touch the back of her hand: "Mingyu, what happened to you? You were fine, yet you’ve fallen so ill. You look like you’ve lost a whole circle of weight, and your complexion is frighteningly poor."

Cui Mingyu leaned against the head of the bed, supported by the soft pillows behind her, and coughed twice in a low voice. Looking at the radiant and spirited Chaogui before her, she could only offer a bitter smile in her heart—all the suffering she had endured was entirely thanks to this princess. Yet Chaogui acted as if she were completely unaware, instead visiting with a face full of concern.

Cui Mingyu knew that if she did not make things clear today, there would surely be more trouble regarding Wei Songjun in the future, and she would only suffer more torment then. She steadied herself, lifted her eyes to look at Chaogui, and spoke in a voice that was soft yet exceptionally clear: "Princess, did you give Prince Jingnan an aphrodisiac?"

The concern on Chaogui’s face paused abruptly, then she nodded candidly, a hint of curiosity in her eyes: "Yes, I did. Why? How did you know about that?"

*So it was true.* A hint of bitterness flashed through Cui Mingyu’s heart. She asked with a wry smile: "Then, Princess, did you also mention to Prince Jingnan... that he is impotent?"

As soon as these words were out, Chaogui was even more surprised. She blinked her almond-shaped eyes, looked Cui Mingyu up and down, and laughed: "Mingyu, why are you so clever today? You could even guess that?"

Cui Mingyu had no heart for jokes; she only felt her throat beginning to ache again. She paused for a moment before saying softly: "It is precisely because of that that Prince Jingnan used the drug on me and trapped me in an ice tub, tormenting me for an entire night."

"What?!" Chaogui’s eyes widened sharply, the smile on her face freezing instantly, replaced by an expression of disbelief: "That fellow Wei Songjun is actually so petty? I was just joking with him, and he took it out on you?"

Seeing her genuine indignation, Cui Mingyu knew she hadn't intended to harm her; she was simply spoiled and acted without considering the consequences. She gritted her teeth, threw off the thin quilt, and struggled to get out of bed.

"Hey? What are you doing?" Chaogui hurriedly reached out to help her, but Cui Mingyu avoided her. She stumbled to the front of the bed and knelt down with a "thud." Her knees hit the cold blue bricks, causing her to frown slightly, yet she kept her spine straight.

"Mingyu! Get up quickly!" Chaogui was anxious and reached out to pull her up.

"If the Princess does not promise me, I will not get up." Cui Mingyu’s voice trembled, but it was exceptionally firm: "I beg the Princess to spare my life. I only wish to live a peaceful life now and never want to have anything to do with Prince Jingnan again. I ask that the Princess never mention Prince Jingnan... and that matter... in front of others again."

Watching her kneeling on the floor, refusing to rise, and seeing her pale face and frail frame, Chaogui’s heart finally softened. She sighed helplessly: "Alright, alright, this Princess promises you! I won't mention it again in the future. Get up quickly, lest you catch another cold."

Only then did Cui Mingyu breathe a sigh of relief. With the help of the hand Chaogui extended, she slowly stood up, returned to the bed, and leaned against the soft pillows, panting.

Watching her exhausted state, Chaogui’s curiosity flared up again. She leaned in, lowered her voice, and asked curiously: "That said, I’ve always been curious: is that fellow Wei Songjun actually... impotent or not?"

Cui Mingyu’s breath, which she had just managed to steady, nearly caught in her throat. Her forehead was instantly covered in black lines. Looking at the "thirst for knowledge" written all over Chaogui’s eyes, she felt a wave of speechlessness and didn't even have the strength to refute her...

chapters.title: Concern
chapters.content:
Qinghe lifted the bamboo curtain and walked in on tiptoe, her nose first catching the faint scent of calming incense in the room. She looked up and saw her mistress, Cui Mingyu, reclining on a soft couch covered in plain silk, while Princess Chaogui sat in a chair nearby. The two were talking, their expressions relaxed and smiling.

With something on her mind, Qinghe paused, unsure whether she should step forward and interrupt. As it happened, Chaogui was just then pressing for information about Prince Jingnan, Wei Songjun. The question sounded exceptionally awkward to Cui Mingyu, who was stammering and looking for an excuse to change the subject when she caught a glimpse of Qinghe in her peripheral vision.

As if grabbing a lifeline, Cui Mingyu immediately raised her voice: "Qinghe, is something the matter?"

Qinghe quickly curtsied and stepped forward, her head slightly bowed and her gaze lowered, her voice respectful and clear: "Mistress, the Second Young Master of the Marquis of Changning’s estate is here. He says he must see you. The Master tried to stop him at the gate for a while, but couldn't, so he sent me to ask for your wishes."

Upon hearing this, Cui Mingyu’s brows knitted almost imperceptibly. She knew her father too well; Father Cui had always felt that Xia Yuning had a wholesome character and had long intended to play matchmaker. It wasn't that he "couldn't stop him," but rather that he was intentionally going with the flow, waiting for her to relent.

She raised a hand to pull the thin quilt around herself, her face still somewhat pale and her voice carrying a hint of weakness: "Look at me, I’m sickly and frail; how can I receive guests? Tell him for me that I will see him once I am feeling better."

"I told him that, Mistress," Qinghe replied truthfully. "But the Second Young Master refuses to leave. He even said... even if he cannot see you in person, he would be content just to hear your voice through the curtain and confirm that you are well."

Cui Mingyu was immediately troubled, her fingertips tapping lightly on the armrest of the couch as she lost her train of thought. Chaogui, however, became interested and leaned in, asking curiously: "Second Young Master Xia? Is that the round-faced little fatty, Xia Yuning, from the Marquis of Changning’s estate? I remember you used to despise him the most and would take a detour whenever you saw him. Why are you hesitating today?"

Cui Mingyu’s face heated up, and she could only offer a dry laugh to smooth things over: "Your Highness is joking. Second Young Master Xia is actually quite a good person; he has a sincere nature and isn't really fat... he just has a bit more meat on his face."

Chaogui was not so easily fooled. She leaned forward slightly, her gaze fixed on Cui Mingyu’s face, her tone probing: "Cui Mingyu, you have been very strange lately. You were never rude to me before, but you were never this polite and considerate either, let alone with Wei Songjun. You used to skip my banquets for his sake. Why have you suddenly decided to let him go, and instead, why are you looking at Xia Yuning—whom you used to look down upon—with such favor? Are you... still yourself?"

Stung by the truth, Cui Mingyu’s dry laugh froze on her face. Seeing Chaogui’s grave expression, she knew she couldn't hide it, so she simply sighed softly and softened her voice: "Your Highness, to tell you the truth, I had a very long dream a while ago. In the dream, I was obsessed with Prince Jingnan, defying my father and offending my friends and family for his sake, only to end up with my family destroyed and my own life in ruins. It was only after I woke up that I truly understood."

She paused, a flash of relief in her eyes: "Since Heaven has given me a chance to start over, why should I cling to someone who doesn't love me? Why not choose someone who cherishes me? Second Young Master Xia is sincere in his intentions, and my father is satisfied with him. If he can truly treat me this way, I am willing to give him a chance, and give myself a chance."

"Choose someone who cherishes you..." Chaogui repeated softly, her eyes unfocused for a moment, as if touched by the words. A moment later, she came back to herself, patted the back of Cui Mingyu’s hand, and smiled: "Even so, don't make a decision too early. There are plenty of fine young men in and around the capital. In a couple of days, when I have time, I’ll take you out to see for yourself; I guarantee you’ll be spoiled for choice."

Cui Mingyu agreed with a smile. Turning to see Qinghe still standing by, waiting, she made up her mind: "Go back to the front hall and tell the Second Young Master that the Princess is here today, so it is truly inconvenient to receive guests. Tell him that once I have recovered, I will accept his invitation to go to Yancui Lake to admire the lotus flowers."

Qinghe acknowledged the order and was about to withdraw when she seemed to remember something and added: "By the way, Mistress, the Second Young Master brought quite a lot of food and tonics when he came, saying they were for your health. Would you like to accept them?"

"Since it is his gesture, accept them," Cui Mingyu nodded, then instructed, "Remember to thank him for his trouble on my behalf."

"Yes." Qinghe withdrew to carry out the order. Before long, she returned carrying a gold-painted lacquer tray. The tray was filled to the brim: a bowl of steaming ginger mutton soup, with fine oil droplets congealing on the edge of the porcelain bowl, the aroma spreading with the steam, rich and enticing; next to it were two plates of exquisite pastries—one of pearly-white yam cakes and one of pale yellow tuckahoe cakes, both exuding a faint scent of rice; in the corner were several sealed jars of bird’s nest and donkey-hide gelatin, clearly carefully selected tonics; and on the very edge of the tray lay a plain envelope that looked exceptionally elegant.

Chaogui leaned over and took a glance, her tone full of approval: "This Xia Yuning is quite thoughtful. He picked things that are both nourishing and appropriate for the season; one can tell he knows how to eat and look after himself. No wonder he’s a little fatty—he’s so attentive to food."

Cui Mingyu had been ill for the past few days and had a poor appetite, but upon smelling the mutton soup, her cravings were instantly piqued, and even her complexion gained a bit of color. She couldn't help but curve her eyes and defend Xia Yuning: "He really isn't fat; he just has a bit of baby fat on his cheeks, which looks quite cute. In another two years, when he grows taller and fills out, he will surely be a dashing figure, perhaps not inferior to anyone in the Princess’s estate."

Chaogui wrinkled her nose and let out a scoff of feigned disdain: "I think he didn't send you mutton soup, but a love potion! Fine, I won't argue with you about this. It’s getting late, so get some good rest. I’ll head back to the estate now and come visit you again another day."

Cui Mingyu rose to see her off, but was pressed back down by Chaogui: "Don't get up, just rest well." With that, she turned and left with her maid.

The room finally quieted down. Cui Mingyu signaled for Qinghe to place the tray on the low table. Her gaze fell on the plain envelope, and she reached out to pick it up. The envelope was not sealed with wax, just simply folded. As she opened it, a small jade pendant slid out.

The pendant was made of top-quality mutton-fat white jade, carved into a lifelike little rabbit. The rabbit’s ears were drooping, and it looked endearingly naive—she was born in the Year of the Rabbit. Cui Mingyu turned the pendant over and saw the two small characters for "Peace" (Ping'an) engraved on the back. The characters were not perfectly rounded, and the strokes carried a certain awkward force, clearly not the work of a professional craftsman—if she wasn't mistaken, this must have been carved by Xia Yuning himself.

She unfolded the letter paper. On it was Xia Yuning’s vigorous yet slightly restrained handwriting, bearing only the four large characters "May you have peace year after year," the brushwork showing a touch of earnestness. At the bottom of the letter were a few additional lines of small text, the ink slightly lighter than the main body, clearly added at the last minute: "Miss Cui, I am somewhat regretful that I could not see you. However, I am overjoyed that you have accepted the invitation to view the lotus flowers. Wishing you a speedy recovery and good health, free from worry."

Though the handwriting was not top-tier, every word was filled with sincerity, warming Cui Mingyu’s heart.

Qinghe, who was tidying up the tray nearby, saw this and said softly: "Mistress, the small text on the letter was added by the Second Young Master on the spot after he asked for brush and ink. He even had a cut on his finger."

Cui Mingyu held the jade rabbit pendant, feeling the warmth of the stone, fearing that his injury had been caused by carving it. She lowered her eyes and replied, "I see."

chapters.title: The Invitation
chapters.content:
The sunlight outside the window filtered through the carved lattice, casting mottled light and shadows on the silk quilt, so warm that one could almost drown in it. Cui Mingyu lay quietly on the couch, her expression one of helplessness.

Eight or nine days had passed since the cold that had nearly cost her half her life. Now, she was fully recovered, her energy flowing smoothly, and she could climb a mountain or go for a run without any trouble. Yet, she insisted on staying securely on the couch, dragging it out day by day; by her count, she had been recuperating for nearly half a month.

She was acting this way only because Wei Songjun had taken a full half-month to recover before appearing in public. She wanted him to know that the suffering she endured was no less than his. Since that was the case, she would also rest for a full half-month—not a minute more, not a second less. This way, he would have no reason to think her suffering was less than his, and they would be even.

From now on, she would owe Wei Songjun nothing, and he would no longer have any claim over her. As for those embarrassing past events, as long as Princess Chaogui could keep her mouth shut and stop gossiping everywhere, then everything would truly be fine, and she could live her own life in peace.

As she was pondering this, a familiar sound of footsteps came from outside the door, carrying a deliberate, cautious lightness. There was no one else it could be but her father, Cui Yong.

As soon as Cui Yong entered, his gaze fell on his daughter on the couch, and his brows immediately furrowed. He walked over and carefully examined Cui Mingyu’s complexion. Seeing her rosy face and clear eyes, with not a trace of illness left, he couldn't help but sigh: "Mingzhu, you are already fully recovered, so why do you keep cooped up in this room? It’s been so many days; if you stay cooped up any longer, I’m afraid you’ll make yourself sick from boredom."

In the past, his daughter had been a restless soul, like a happy little bird, thinking about running out all day long, or inviting three or five friends to tour the lake, or going for an outing in the suburbs, living a lively life. Back then, he had worried that her nature was too wild and that she lacked the decorum of a lady of a noble house. But now that she was staying quietly at home, he was even more worried, feeling that the girl had something weighing on her heart, making her unnaturally quiet.

Cui Mingyu looked up at him, her voice soft and gentle: "Father, I think this is quite good. It’s quiet and peaceful, and it doesn't take much effort."

"What’s good about it!" Cui Yong waved his hand in disapproval. "Young people should go out more, meet people, and get some fresh air. It pains me to see you cooped up like this." He paced the room twice, as if he had suddenly remembered something. His eyes lit up, and he took a silver-patterned invitation from his sleeve and handed it to Cui Mingyu: "Look, what is this?"

Cui Mingyu reached out and took it, her fingertips touching the delicate silk of the invitation. She saw that it was written in elegant small regular script, with the signature "Xu Estate." After a moment of thought, she remembered—it was the recently retired Grand Secretary Xu, formerly the Grand Tutor Xu, who was holding a poetry gathering at his home.

Although this poetry gathering had a grand reputation, claiming to be a place to make friends through poetry and exchange literary talents, those with any connections in the capital knew the unspoken truth: Grand Tutor Xu was simply restless and was using the gathering as a pretext to play matchmaker for the eligible young men and women of the noble families.

Cui Mingyu was well aware of the original owner's level of poetic skill; she could barely manage a few lines, which was hardly impressive—one might even call it mediocre. Furthermore, the Prince of Jingnan, Wei Songjun, never attended such lively occasions. In the past, she would naturally decline whenever possible, never intending to join in the festivities.

Yet, this time, her father had accepted the invitation.

Holding the invitation, Cui Mingyu looked at Cui Yong with a sense of helplessness. "Father, it’s not as if you don’t know that your daughter doesn't have much ink in her belly. Going to a poetry gathering would only be an embarrassment, wouldn't it?"

Cui Yong chuckled, completely unbothered. "Embarrassment? It’s the participation that counts! We aren't going to compete for the top prize; we’re just going to relax, enjoy the scenery, and chat with other young ladies. You’ve been cooped up at home for a while now, and I think you’re about to go stir-crazy." He shifted his tone, his eyes glinting with a hint of craftiness. "Besides, didn't you say you didn't think much of that Xia boy? Who knows, you might meet a young man more to your liking at the gathering! There are plenty of talented men in the capital; you can't just hang yourself from a single tree."

Cui Mingyu gave a faint, mocking smile to herself. Who said she didn't think much of the Xia boy? She merely wanted to see how long his so-called sincerity would last. After all, affection in this capital was mostly as thin as a cicada's wing, unable to withstand scrutiny.

However, since her father had good intentions and had specifically accepted the invitation, she would be slighting him if she insisted on refusing. After a moment of contemplation, Cui Mingyu nodded. "Since Father has said so, your daughter will go."

Seeing her agreement, Cui Yong’s face beamed with joy. He gave a few more instructions for her to prepare well before heading off happily.

Once Cui Yong left, Cui Mingyu placed the invitation on a small side table and said to her maid, Qinghe, who was standing by, "Qinghe, go and find out if Princess Chaogui will be attending Grand Tutor Xu’s poetry gathering."

Qinghe was stunned for a moment, then replied, "Yes, Miss. But... doesn't Princess Chaogui usually dislike these kinds of poetry gatherings?"

Indeed. Princess Chaogui’s status was quite unique; she had been widowed at a young age and kept male companions, which always made things somewhat awkward in the eyes of the capital's noble families. She herself couldn't be bothered to involve herself in these gatherings of noble ladies for fear of gossip, and she had never once attended Grand Tutor Xu’s gatherings in the past.

"Go and ask, and you shall know," Cui Mingyu said. She had her own calculations: if Princess Chaogui didn't go, the gathering would just be a place for her to relax; but if the Princess did attend, she would have to be more cautious to avoid any unnecessary trouble.

Not daring to delay, Qinghe went off to inquire immediately.

Before long, Qinghe returned with a look of novelty on her face. "Miss, I’ve found out! When Princess Chaogui heard you were going to attend, she actually said she wanted to come and 'keep an eye on things' for you. She has already agreed to go!"

Cui Mingyu was somewhat surprised, then understood. Princess Chaogui had always loved a bit of excitement, especially when it concerned her. She likely thought it was amusing that someone who "didn't have much ink in her belly" dared to attend a poetry gathering, and wanted to come and see for herself.

Very well, let her come. She wasn't afraid.

Two days later, news of Grand Tutor Xu’s poetry gathering became even more of a sensation in the capital, as word spread that Mu Wanzhou, the daughter of the Prime Minister, would also be attending.

Mu Wanzhou was the renowned "First Talented Woman" of the Great Qi. Not only was she breathtakingly beautiful, but she was also proficient in poetry, songs, music, chess, calligraphy, and painting—the ideal partner in the hearts of countless noble youths. She usually kept to herself and rarely attended such gatherings; now that she had agreed to attend Grand Tutor Xu’s event, how could people not be excited?

When Cui Mingyu heard this name, her fingertips paused slightly. She remembered clearly that in the original novel she had transmigrated into, Mu Wanzhou was the official love interest of the male lead, Wei Songjun.

In the original story, the original owner had been foolish and drugged Wei Songjun, causing him to lose most of his internal energy and nearly causing a catastrophe. Later, it was Mu Wanzhou who exhausted all her efforts to find a rare, miraculous medicine that allowed Wei Songjun to recover. It was precisely because of this kindness that the two gradually came to know and love each other, creating a legendary romance.

But now, because of her arrival, the trajectory of the original book had already changed. Wei Songjun hadn't lost his internal energy that day, so what would become of the catalyst for his and Mu Wanzhou’s meeting?

Cui Mingyu felt a bit dazed, wondering what kind of aftermath this butterfly effect would bring.

Mu Wanzhou’s attendance made the poetry gathering impossible to get into. Many noble youths who were originally uninterested in the event were now pulling strings to get an invitation just to catch a glimpse of the talented Miss Mu. Speculators were even driving the price of invitations for male guests to astronomical heights, yet demand still outstripped supply.

Looking at the three-inch-wide invitation for female guests in her hand, Cui Mingyu suddenly had a thought—if she sold this, could she trade it for some silver?

Although her father, Cui Yong, was the Minister of Revenue and held great power with a substantial family fortune, he was extremely strict with money and kept her monthly allowance on a tight leash, claiming he was afraid she would develop a spendthrift nature—it was as if he had caught an occupational disease from being the Minister of Revenue. If she could save up some silver of her own, it would be more convenient for her to act in the future.

Her maid, Bitao, saw her staring at the invitation in a trance and leaned in, whispering, "Miss, don't overthink it. The invitations for this gathering have different colors for men and women; the men’s are gold-stamped red, while the women’s are silver-patterned pink, and they aren't worth anything. Besides, many young ladies heard that Miss Mu was going and are now afraid of being overshadowed, so they don't even want to go!"
